$note: Written after rendering the reel and looking at full-resolution stills from it — not from the contact sheet, which is an overview and not an inspection. Scores are one person's judgement out of ten and are deliberately NOT computed: every reel this repo has shipped broken passed the computed gates.
question: How Was a Medieval Sword Actually Made?
verdict: The process reads and now the object does too. One outline persists across every stage, and it keeps its VOLUME: drawing it out makes it longer and thinner, folding makes it shorter and thicker, so by the quench it is a blade rather than the stubby wedge every stage used to be. Metal carries a specular line the other materials do not earn, and the heat tint means hot iron looks hot instead of looking like frosted glass. The one wrong drawing in the reel is gone: a claim about a sword snapping is no longer illustrated with a megalith on rollers.
whatWorked: Conservation of volume is a general rule about worked stock, and it is what made the object legible.
Each stage names both its state and its cause: FOLDED / THE LAYERS DOUBLE.
The haulage drawing now refuses a line with nothing to move, so it cannot be the last thing standing.
whatFailed: Camera variety is the lowest of the five: a single centred object on a dark ground gives the camera little to reframe.
Seven lines fall to typography, the most of any episode.
The agent — hammer, tongs, quench — is small and brief against the blade.

remainingDefects.what: No photograph of a real blade or a real forge
